[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
George Glasgow appears among Royal Artillery colonels in June 1811.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050144942/ Freeman’s Journal, 10 June 1811, p. 4], original previously inspected on 4 October 2026.</ref> A War Office notice in September 1819 lists Major-General George Glasgow of the Royal Artillery among officers taking lieutenant-general rank by brevet.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050057308/ Freeman’s Journal, 6 September 1819, p. 4], original previously inspected on 4 October 2026.</ref>

John W. Spurr’s biography records his appointment as an artillery cadet on 2 April 1771, colonel in 1806, major-general in July 1811 and lieutenant-general in August 1819. It gives his death as 28 October 1820 in London and names his late wife Margaret Green.<ref>[https://www.biographi.ca/en/bio/glasgow_george_5E.html John W. Spurr, “GLASGOW, GEORGE,” Dictionary of Canadian Biography, vol. 5], full English entry read on 17 October 2026.</ref>

The likely burial entry for this officer records George Glasgow, aged 64, buried on 3 November 1820 at St Luke, Charlton by Greenwich, Kent. Two companion indexes supply the lieutenant-general title; Woolwich is recorded as residence. The age implies a birth about 1756, not an exact birthday. These are three index forms of one burial, and the original register has not been inspected.<ref>[https://findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=GBPRS%2FD%2F28050276&tab=this Findmypast GBPRS/D/28050276 — St Luke Charlton burial derivative transcript]; [https://findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=BMD%2FNBI%2F12413020 Findmypast BMD/NBI/12413020 — St Luke Charlton burial derivative transcript]; [https://findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=GBPRS%2FD%2F963049679%2F1&tab=this Findmypast GBPRS/D/963049679/1 — St Luke Charlton burial derivative transcript], derivative transcripts inspected 23 October 2026; probably the same officer by title, locality and chronology.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

The full DCB entry, successfully read through urllib on 17 October, identifies a cadet appointed 2 April 1771, colonel from 24 July 1806, major-general from 4 July 1811, lieutenant-general in August 1819, died 28 October 1820. This joins the June 1811 colonel and September 1819 brevet notices. Actual candidate biographies exclude 1529 (baptised 1769, aged two at cadet appointment), 3611 (born 1777, died 1857) and 3345 (born 1792). Retain the documented 6 October fully paged George/variant duplicate audit; no compatible profile found. Earlier 1771 first-lieutenant evidence describes another officer and must not be conflated with this 1771 cadet.

The English DCB says London; its French search snippet says Charlton, Gloucestershire. Keep the exact death place qualified. The earlier 1771 first lieutenant is not this officer’s cadet appointment.

Burial on 3 November is distinct from death on 28 October. Charlton is the burial place; it does not resolve the retained London/Charlton death-place question.

=== Earlier possible artillery family assessment — superseded by will review ===
Edward George, husband of Emily Caroline Medlicott, is a possible son of General George Glasgow, assessed at 55%. The compiled Glasgow–Green family lists an Edward George at Quebec in 1794 alongside George Mark in 1795. George Mark’s independent obituary identifies his father as the late General Glasgow of the same artillery corps. The held OCR of The Spectator, 1 March 1851, calls George Mark a son of the late General Glasgow of the same corps.<ref>[https://archive.org/details/sim_spectator-uk_1851-03-01_24_1183 The Spectator, 1 March 1851, deaths column], held OCR reading; original page not inspected in this review.</ref> The two sons’ unusual full names and Quebec setting favour this family over an unspecified London parent. The compiled child’s identification with the adult husband remains unproved. No maternal identity or merger with the separate 1843 death account is assigned.<ref>[https://www.oocities.org/Athens/7734/dat28.htm#4 Compiled Glasgow–Green family], unsourced compilation; [https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/D199415 The National Archives, will catalogue D199415, PROB11/1637/234], original will uninspected.</ref>

=== Confident son William, Bengal officer ===
General George Glasgow is the newly selected confident father of William Glasgow in the Bengal William-and-Amelia household, assessed at 95%. Hodson’s printed officer biography explicitly calls William the son of George Glasgow of Greenwich, lieutenant-general Royal Artillery. It records William’s marriage to Amelia Campbell at Barrackpore on 15 October 1824. The held baptism index places William and Amelia’s first known child William at Barrackpore on 6 September 1825, followed by the same parental names at other Bengal stations. This specific wife, station and chronology identifies the officer with the existing documentary father far more securely than name and Bengal alone. The general’s name, rank, corps, Greenwich residence and Quebec service identify the existing General George account. This is a new named father for an already catalogued family, not a first numerical rating of a previously selected father. The 95% is a subjective estimate of the whole father-profile identification, not a measured frequency. The printed 1928 biography was visually inspected; its underlying cadet, marriage and burial originals were not. Hodson states the officer’s parentage directly, while transferring it to the baptism-index household remains an identity inference. It names no mother for William. No Green mother, identity merge or new WikiTree profile is selected. Amelia Glasgow-482’s separate 78% identification and Edward George’s separate 55% father assessment are unchanged. The officer’s 1841 death distinguishes him from the separate 53rd Native Infantry William described as murdered in February 1855; that service file remains unread and is not attached to this father.<ref>[https://archive.org/details/dli.csl.3669/page/n278/mode/1up V. C. P. Hodson, List of the Officers of the Bengal Army, 1758–1834, part II (1928), p.273, William Glasgow]. Printed page visually inspected 12 November 2026; underlying historical originals unread.</ref>

=== Original will review — 12 November 2026 ===
General George Glasgow is the probable father of Edward George Glasgow, husband of Emily Caroline Medlicott, at 78% subjective confidence, increased from 55%. The general’s original registered will explicitly includes Edward George Glasgow among his children, alongside George Mark and William. It therefore independently verifies the distinctive family group previously known from an unsourced compilation. The existing adult account has the same uncommon full name and an 1823 military marriage; the general’s Canadian family, London connections and the chronology are compatible. This is a material Possible-to-Probable improvement from a newly read original, not a first numerical rating. The will proves that the general had a son named Edward George, but does not name Emily Caroline, state Edward’s age, or identify his regiment. Identification with the 1823 groom and Bermondsey/Dover father remains an inference. Conflicting index ages and the separate 1843 death identity remain unresolved; no birth/death field, mother, identity merge or new WikiTree profile is selected. The general’s own parents are still Unknown. William’s separate 95% connection is unchanged.<ref>[https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/D199415 The National Archives, PROB 11/1637/234, will of George Glasgow, dated 28 October 1818, proved 16 December 1820]. Original registered will, downloaded PDF pp.1–2 visually inspected 12 November 2026.</ref>

George Glasgow, lieutenant-general in the Royal Artillery, then residing in Trinity Place, Charing Cross, made his will on 28 October 1818. It names Edward George, George Mark and William among his children and provides separate shares in property in Canada/British North America for named children. The will was proved at London on 16 December 1820; William Shaw is identified as one executor. This is a selective factual abstract, not a complete transcription. Both downloaded PDF pages were inspected; the second continues the attestation and probate before beginning another testator’s will. No parent of the testator was identified in his will.
